summary: Darunavir is an HIV-1 protease inhibitor that must always be boosted with ritonavir or cobicistat and combined with other antiretrovirals to treat HIV-1 in adults and children >=3 years (and >=10 kg). It is taken with food. Key risks are drug-induced hepatitis (monitor liver chemistries) and severe skin reactions (it contains a sulfonamide moiety); it has extensive CYP3A-mediated drug interactions and many contraindicated co-medications.
indications: Treatment of HIV-1 infection, co-administered with ritonavir and other antiretroviral agents, in adults and pediatric patients 3 years of age and older (weighing at least 10 kg)

moa: Darunavir is a selective inhibitor of HIV-1 protease. It binds the protease active site and prevents cleavage of viral Gag-Pol polyprotein precursors, blocking formation of mature infectious virions. It retains activity against many protease inhibitor-resistant strains owing to high binding affinity. It is co-administered with ritonavir or cobicistat, which inhibit CYP3A to boost darunavir plasma concentrations.

absolute: Co-administration with drugs highly dependent on CYP3A whose raised levels cause serious events: alfuzosin, dronedarone, ivabradine, ranolazine, ergot derivatives (dihydroergotamine, ergotamine, methylergonovine), lurasidone, pimozide, oral midazolam, triazolam, lovastatin, simvastatin, lomitapide, sildenafil for PAH, naloxegol, elbasvir/grazoprevir, colchicine in renal/hepatic impairment
Rifampin and St. John's wort (reduce darunavir efficacy)
relative: Pre-existing hepatic disease (chronic hepatitis B/C, cirrhosis, raised transaminases)

preg: Recommended regimen in pregnancy is darunavir 600 mg with ritonavir 100 mg twice daily with food; the once-daily regimen is not recommended because of lower exposure. Use as part of guideline-based ART.
lact: In the United States, breastfeeding is not recommended for women living with HIV-1 because of the potential for HIV transmission and adverse effects.
renal: No dose adjustment is needed for darunavir in renal impairment. (Note that contraindicated co-medications such as colchicine apply in renal impairment.)
hepatic: Not recommended in severe hepatic impairment (no data). Use with caution in mild to moderate impairment; drug-induced hepatitis, including fatal cases, has occurred - monitor liver chemistries.

major: Strong CYP3A substrates with narrow index (see contraindications)
CYP3A inducers - rifampin, St. John's wort, carbamazepine, phenytoin (reduce darunavir levels)

Other agents needing dose changes: rifabutin, certain statins (atorvastatin/rosuvastatin lowest dose), many antiarrhythmics, immunosuppressants (tacrolimus, cyclosporine), DOACs (rivaroxaban/apixaban), corticosteroids (inhaled/systemic - Cushing risk)
moderate: Combined hormonal contraceptives (efficacy reduced - use alternative/additional method)
Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors for erectile dysfunction (limit dose)
interactions.food: Must be taken with food - food increases darunavir exposure significantly
interactions.alcohol: No direct interaction; limit because of hepatotoxicity potential
interactions.diagnostics: May raise transaminases, glucose, triglycerides and cholesterol

serious: Severe skin reactions: Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis

monitoring: Serum liver chemistries before and during therapy (more frequently with underlying liver disease)
Skin reactions, especially early in therapy
HIV RNA viral load and CD4 count for response; resistance testing in experienced patients
counsel: Always take with ritonavir (or cobicistat) and with food - the drug does not work alone
Do not start any new medicine, supplement (especially St. John's wort), or recreational drug without checking for interactions
Report yellowing of skin/eyes, dark urine, or right-sided abdominal pain (liver problems)
Stop and seek care for any rash with blistering, fever, or facial swelling
Hormonal birth control may not work - use an additional/alternative method
Do not stop or skip doses - this can cause resistance
pk: Plasma levels achieved promptly when boosted and taken with food
Approximately 15 hours when co-administered with ritonavir
Supports once- or twice-daily boosted dosing
Store at 25 C (excursions 15-30 C); keep tablets in original container
pearls: MUST be boosted with ritonavir or cobicistat and combined with other ARVs - never used as the sole or unboosted PI
Drug-induced hepatitis (sometimes fatal) and severe skin reactions are the key safety signals - monitor LFTs and counsel on rash
Contains a sulfonamide moiety - use caution in sulfonamide allergy
Huge CYP3A interaction list with many absolute contraindications (statins, ergots, certain sedatives, rifampin, St. John's wort) - always check co-medications
missed: If you miss a dose and it is within 6 hours (twice-daily) or 12 hours (once-daily) of the missed time, take it with food right away. If more time has passed, skip it and take the next dose at the usual time with food - do not double up.
overdose: There is no specific antidote. Management is supportive with monitoring of vital signs, liver function and clinical status. Because darunavir is highly protein-bound, dialysis is unlikely to remove significant drug. Treat hypersensitivity or hepatotoxicity supportively.
